title: Repositories, keys and universal packages
summary: Where packages come from, how signatures protect you, and snaps, flatpaks and AppImages.

steps.title: Repositories and signing keys
body: A **repository** is a web server with packages plus a signed index. Configuration lives in:
RHEL/Fedora    /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo                          keys: rpm --import <url>, gpgkey= in the .repo
Arch           /etc/pacman.conf  (+ the AUR, community build scripts: use a helper like yay, read PKGBUILDs)
Alpine         /etc/apk/repositories   (main, community; edge/testing for new things)

Adding a third-party Debian repo, the modern way: download the vendor's key into `/etc/apt/keyrings/vendor.gpg`, then a source with `Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/vendor.gpg`, so that key can only sign **that** repo. (The old `apt-key add` trusted a key for every repo and is deprecated.)
The package manager refuses unsigned or wrongly signed indexes: `NO_PUBKEY`, `GPG check FAILED`. Never "fix" that by disabling checks; get the right key from the vendor over HTTPS.

steps.prompt: `apt update` fails with `The following signatures couldn't be verified because the public key is not available: NO_PUBKEY 1234ABCD`. What is the right fix?
options: Install the vendor's signing key into /etc/apt/keyrings and reference it with Signed-By in that repo's source
steps.explain: Disabling verification means anyone who can tamper with the download can install code as root on your machine.

steps.title: Snaps, flatpaks and AppImages
body: Universal formats ship an app **with its dependencies**, the same file on every distro:
| backed by | Canonical (Snap Store) | community (Flathub) | nobody: a single file |
| good for | desktop **and** server/CLI apps, IoT (Ubuntu Core) | desktop GUI apps | portable desktop apps |
| sandbox | AppArmor confinement | bubblewrap / portals | none by default |
| updates | automatic, by snapd | `flatpak update` | manual (or the app itself) |
| command | `snap install code --classic` | `flatpak install flathub org.gimp.GIMP` | `chmod +x App.AppImage && ./App.AppImage` |
Trade-offs: bigger downloads and disk use, slower first start (snaps), and less integration with the system. On servers, prefer distro packages or containers.

steps.prompt: Add a vendor's apt repository with a key that is only trusted for that repository.
code: echo "deb [signed-by=__1__] https://vendor.example/apt stable main" | sudo tee __2__
steps.explain: Scoping the key with signed-by prevents it from vouching for packages in other repositories.

steps.prompt: A blog post says to install a tool on Arch with `yay -S some-tool` from the AUR. What should you do first?
options: Read the PKGBUILD: AUR packages are community build scripts that run on your machine, not vetted repository packages
Nothing: the AUR is the official repository
Run it with sudo so it can install system-wide
steps.explain: The AUR is convenient and huge, but anyone can upload to it. Helpers like yay show the PKGBUILD so you can check what it downloads and runs.

steps.title: Pick the package manager
prompt: Write `string PackageManager(Dictionary<string, string> os)` from parsed `/etc/os-release` fields:
- Look at `ID` then each word of `ID_LIKE` (lowercase) and use the first that is known:
- `rhel`, `centos`, `rocky`, `almalinux` → `"dnf"`, but `"yum"` when `VERSION_ID`'s major number is below 8
Note the version rule applies to whichever of `ID` or `ID_LIKE` matched (CentOS 7 has `ID="centos"`, `VERSION_ID="7"`).
solution: int major = int.TryParse((version ?? "").Split('.')[0], out var m) ? m : 0;
case "rhel": case "centos": case "rocky": case "almalinux": return major > 0 && major < 8 ? "yum" : "dnf";
hints: Collect ID then the ID_LIKE words; return on the first known one.
template: Dictionary<string, string> Os(params string[] kv) { var d = new Dictionary<string, string>(); for (int i = 0; i < kv.Length; i += 2) d[kv[i]] = kv[i + 1]; return d; }
